extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer officers, university legal counsel, patent attorneys, and technology managers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal/regulatory criteria governing university technology transfer, including patent, copyright, trademark, international treaties, and mask-work (semiconductor) protection — aimed at guiding institutional practice and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayh-Dole Act (P.L. 96-517) — key provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bayh-Dole Act (effective July 1981) established a uniform federal patent policy enabling universities to elect to retain title to inventions conceived or reduced to practice using government funding and encouraged collaboration with commercial concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific provisions include: establishment of a uniform federal patent policy; universities may elect to retain title; universities must file patent applications on inventions they elect to own; the government retains a nonexclusive license to practice the invention for governmental purposes; government retains march-in rights; preference in licensing to small business; provision of uniform guidelines for granting licenses; and preference for U.S. industry. The Act is the statutory authority for agencies to take title to and hold patents in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-124 — implementation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB Circular A-124 (Feb 10, 1982) issued policy guidance to federal agencies for implementing Bayh-Dole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarified: standard patent rights clauses for use in federal funding agreements; reporting requirements for universities electing title; and special federal rights in inventions. Codified at 37 CFR Part 401.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government Patent Policy (Presidential Memorandum) — extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A Presidential Memorandum (Feb 18, 1983) mandated broad application of the new government patent policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directed federal agencies to extend Bayh-Dole terms to all government contractors (not only universities, nonprofits, and small businesses) and led to amendments to the Federal Acquisition Regulations (FAR) to assure implementation across R&D agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Law 98-620 — amendments to Bayh-Dole
rubrics_metrics.description: P.L. 98-620 (Nov 8, 1984) amended the original Bayh-Dole Act to remove certain restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notably deleted the term limitation on exclusive licenses and substituted the Secretary of Commerce for the Comptroller General to determine “exceptional circumstances” when contractor rights might be overruled; these amendments reduced politically motivated constraints in the original act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Commerce final rules (37 CFR Part 401) — implementing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules published March 18, 1987 (codified at 37 CFR Part 401.1-401.16) finalized implementation of Bayh-Dole, P.L. 98-620, OMB Circular, and the Presidential Memorandum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules specify the rights and obligations of all parties and constitute the operating manual for modern technology transfer officers; they should be consulted for procedural and compliance details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stevenson-Wydler Technology Innovation Act and Federal Technology Transfer Act (FTTA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stevenson-Wydler (P.L. 96-480) as amended by FTTA (15 U.S.C. 3710) authorized government-operated federal laboratories to enter into cooperative research and development agreements (CRADAs) with various public and private entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits CRADAs with state/local governments, industry (corporations, partnerships), public/private organizations (including universities), nonprofits, private individuals (including licensees of agency-owned inventions), and other federal agencies. FTTA language parallels Bayh-Dole and facilitates federal lab–industry–university collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act — effects on enforcement and foreign filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act (Aug 23, 1988) strengthened IP enforcement and eased certain foreign-filing burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects described include: preventing offshore practice of patented processes followed by importation without liability; strengthening remedies (easier exclusion orders from U.S. ITC); pressuring foreign countries to enact/enforce IP laws; expanding scope of foreign-filing licenses to permit subsequent modifications/amendments/supplements (but not when they change the nature of the invention or disclose national security information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 337 of the Tariff Act — import-related IP enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: New Section 337 made unlawful the importation into or sale in the U.S. of articles that infringe U.S. patents, copyrights, trademarks, or semiconductor mask works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives IP owners stronger remedies to block infringing imports, including ITC exclusion orders; applies to patented goods or goods made by patented processes, infringing trademarks, and semiconductor chips that infringe registered mask works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 301 of the Trade Act — U.S. trade representative enforcement process
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 301 provides a mechanism to exert pressure on foreign countries that deny adequate and effective IP protection or fair market access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires submission of evidence of international piracy to the U.S. Trade Representative, who may list offending countries in the Federal Register and initiate investigations (to be completed within 18 months) and recommend sanctions to the President for unjustifiable or discriminatory trade practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: CREATE Act (P.L. 108-453) — collaborative research and obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act (Dec 10, 2004) amended 35 U.S.C. 103(c) so patentability is not precluded because of collaborative research conducted among researchers employed by different organizations, treating them as a single entity for prior art purposes when a joint research agreement exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to promote collaborative research, reduce chilling effects of derived prior art (overruling Oddzon v. Just Toys concerns), decrease litigation, and encourage cooperation; USPTO issued special rules implementing CREATE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright statutory framework — Title 17 and Copyright Act of 1976
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Constitution authorizes Congress to write copyright laws; Title 17 contains statutory provisions. The Copyright Act of 1976 (effective Jan 1, 1978) substantially revised prior law to address new technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: federal statutory protection upon fixation for unpublished and published works; registration is not required to obtain copyright protection (fixation suffices); divisibility of exclusive rights allows transfer of subsets of rights; some gaps remain for works not fixed in a tangible medium (e.g., extemporaneous performances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Berne Convention Implementation Act (BCIA) of 1988 — international harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: BCIA (1988) allowed U.S. accession to the Berne Convention and removed certain formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminated the requirement of a copyright notice upon publication (placing all copyrightable subject matter under protection), and eliminated the requirement of pre-litigation registration for foreign works (not for U.S. works). The Berne Convention also recognizes moral rights, although the U.S. did not expressly expand its statute to fully mirror Berne's moral-rights language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Artists Rights Act (VARA) of 1990 — moral rights for visual artists
rubrics_metrics.description: VARA (effective June 1, 1991) created certain moral rights for authors of paintings, sculptures, and prints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives lifetime rights (with exceptions) to (1) receive credit as author, (2) prevent use of the author’s name on works not created by the author, and (3) prevent intentional mutilation/distortion/modification (or to prevent use of author’s name on such modified works) when such changes would harm the author's reputation (17 U.S.C. § 106A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark statutory framework — Lanham Act and subsequent revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark protection evolved from early acts (1905) through the Lanham Act (1946) and later revisions (Trademark Law Revision Act of 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lanham Act provided registration of trademarks used in interstate commerce, service marks, certification marks, possibility of incontestability under conditions, and cancellation for non-use (e.g., failure to file affidavit of use within six years). The 1989 Revision Act permits filing for trademark protection in anticipation of interstate commerce. NAFTA and other treaties also affect geographic indicators and related trademark rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: NAFTA and international IP treaty obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: NAFTA (Dec 17, 1992) and related international conventions require member countries to meet minimum IP protection and enforcement standards and to give effect to substantive provisions of conventions (e.g., Paris, Berne, UPOV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NAFTA's Chapter 17 establishes obligations including right of priority (Paris Convention), patent-term provisions (patent term as 20 years from filing or 17 from issue, whichever is longer), and other minimum protections; member states had to adjust domestic law to conform to NAFTA requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: GATT-TRIPs (Uruguay Round) — trade-related IP standards
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPs (under GATT Uruguay Round) requires GATT signatory countries to provide certain patent protections and enforcement mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant provisions include: patent term of 20 years from earliest filed application (with limited extensions for special circumstances); ability to use provisional applications (establish priority without claims); patent rights include exclusive right to offer for sale and to import patented goods; rules affecting interference proof of invention date across signatory countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Inventor's Protection Act (AIPA) — broad patent reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: AIPA (1999) enacted many patent-system reforms with direct impact on university technology transfer (described as the most significant changes since 1952).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIPA introduced patent-term adjustment, 18-month publication of applications, reexamination reform (inter partes participation and estoppel consequences), and prior-user rights among other changes; these provisions affect prosecution strategy, publication risk, and litigation posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Term Adjustment (AIPA) — statutory guarantees and adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: AIPA provides three bases for patent-term adjustment (PTO failures to act within statutory timeframes; PTO failure to issue patent within three years of filing; and delays due to interference, secrecy orders, or successful appellate review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides day-for-day adjustments for each failure/delay and guarantees a minimum patent term of seventeen years from issuance. Applicants must make reasonable efforts to conclude examination because applicant-caused delays can offset adjustments; nevertheless, applicant will receive at least twenty years from filing date (subject to adjustments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteen-Month Publication (AIPA) — publication and provisional rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIPA, U.S. patent applications filed after Nov 29, 2000, may be published 18 months after filing (with certain exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: design applications; applications under secrecy order; provisional applications; applications where applicant requests non-publication provided no foreign filing requiring publication; and filing of a Request for Continued Examination does not prevent publication. Published applications become prior art and searchable; provisional rights may allow recovery of reasonable royalty for acts between publication and issuance if the infringer had actual notice of the published application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination reforms (AIPA) — third-party participation and estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: AIPA reformed reexamination procedures to allow a third-party requesting reexamination (for patents issuing from applications filed on or after Nov 29, 1999) to participate to a limited extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party requestor can file one written comment on each PTO action and applicant response, can appeal to the Board of Appeals of the PTO (but not directly to federal circuit), and is estopped from later raising issues they 'raised or could have raised' in the reexamination. Requestor is estopped from later challenging any fact determined in reexamination. Patent owner may appeal final rejection of claims to the Board or federal court and can seek a stay in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-User Rights (AIPA) — defense for prior commercial use
rubrics_metrics.description: AIPA created a defense to patent infringement for certain methods of doing or conducting business practiced prior to the patentee's filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense is limited to methods of doing or conducting business (e.g., financial and e-commerce patents). The alleged infringer must have practiced the method at least one year before the patentee filed its application and commercially exploited the method before the patentee filed its patent application. A patent will not be considered invalid because of assertion of the prior-use defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work exclusive rights (Semiconductor Chip Protection Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner of a mask work has exclusive rights to: (1) reproduce the mask work by optical, electronic, or any other means; (2) import or distribute a semiconductor chip product in which the mask work is embodied; and (3) induce or knowingly cause another person to reproduce the mask work or import/distribute a semiconductor product embodying the mask work. (17 U.S.C. §§ 901-914)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusive rights are narrower/shorter in duration than patent or copyright and should be considered alongside other protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work reverse engineering limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse engineering of a mask work is permitted and provides an affirmative defense to infringement if done legitimately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse engineering is allowed solely for the purposes of teaching, analyzing, or evaluating the concepts or techniques embodied in the mask work or in the circuitry, logic flow, or organization of components used in the mask work. If legitimate, the results may be incorporated into an original mask work which may be distributed (17 U.S.C. § 906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work first sale doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasers of semiconductor chips have the right to use and resell them freely under the Chip Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, purchasers may not reproduce chips without permission of the mask-work owner; the first-sale right does not permit reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work loss of rights — registration deadline and expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: If registration of a mask work does not occur within two years of its first commercial exploitation, the right to mask-work protection will be lost; rights are also lost after expiration of the registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely registration is critical; the two-year window and the finite statutory term make strategic timing of registration important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work duration and effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: Mask-work protection lasts for a ten-year time period beginning on the earlier of (1) the date the mask work is registered with the U.S. Copyright Office or (2) the date the mask work is first commercially exploited anywhere in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ten-year period expires at the end of the calendar year in which protection would otherwise expire; this finite duration affects commercialization and enforcement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work ownership rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive rights in a mask work belong to the person who created the mask work (or legal representative) or to a party to whom all rights have been transferred by written instrument. If made within scope of employment, the owner is the employer unless rights are transferred by written instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership is analogous to copyright; written assignments are required to transfer rights and institutional policies/contractual terms govern ownership assertions in employer/employee contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work requirements for protection: originality and fixation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mask-work protection requires both originality and fixation: a design is original if independently created and more than merely staple/commonplace variations; fixation occurs once the mask work is sufficiently permanent or stable to permit perception or reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection does not extend to ideas, procedures, processes, systems, methods of operation, concepts, principles, or discoveries. The originality requirement excludes staple/commonplace designs 'or variations of such designs' unless, considered as a whole, they are original (17 U.S.C. § 902(b)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work registration procedure and deposit requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To register a mask work with the U.S. Copyright Office, Form MW, filing fee, and deposit are required; the deposit requirement depends on whether the mask work has been commercially exploited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For commercially exploited mask works: four chips as first commercially exploited plus one full set of visually perceptible reproductions of each layer (plastic color overlays, composite plots, or photographs). For non-commercially exploited works: one full set of overlays or plots, optionally reproductions of most complete fixed form. See 37 C.F.R. § 211.5 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work notice — optional but evidentiary
rubrics_metrics.description: Affixing a notice to mask works and semiconductor chip products is not required but serves as prima facie evidence of notice of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of appropriate notices include textual and symbolic forms (e.g., 'Mask work Iowa State University', '*M* Iowa State University', 'M Iowa State University'). Use of notice supports enforcement though it is not a prerequisite for protection (17 U.S.C. § 909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work remedies — enforcement and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: After receipt of a certificate of registration, the owner or exclusive licensee may bring a civil action for infringement occurring after commencement of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available remedies include statutory damages up to $250,000, or alternatively actual damages or infringer's profits attributable to the infringement. Few reported cases exist (e.g., Brooktree v. AMD), so statutory scheme and strategy should be reviewed carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work transfer of rights and recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership rights may be transferred or licensed in whole or in part by a written, signed instrument; assignments and licenses may be recorded in the U.S. Copyright Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers must be in writing and signed by owner; recording provides public notice and is normal practice for institutional transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work international protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Other countries may provide equivalent or similar protection for semiconductors and mask works but not all countries have registration requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should evaluate country-specific rules for mask-work-like protection and consider complementary protections (patents, copyrights) for broader, longer-term global coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask-work practical considerations for technology managers
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial exploitation timing affects registration deadline and duration; registration prior to commercial exploitation starts the 10-year clock; not all semiconductors are protectable (direct-writing techniques may preclude mask-work protection); other forms of protection (patent, copyright) may be preferable or complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: weigh useful lifespan of technology vs 10-year term; consider registering shortly before commercial exploitation if longer term is needed; evaluate whether mask-work protection materially supplements (or should be supplemented by) patents or copyrights.
